item.title: Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
item.description:
The Single Responsibility Principle #

What Is the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)? #

The Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) states that there should never be more than one reason for a class to change.

For example, consider the design shown below.

classDiagram
Computational Geometry Application --> Rectangle
Graphical Application --> Rectangle
Graphical Application --> GUI
Rectangle --> GUI
class Rectangle {
 +void draw()
 +double area()
}

The Rectangle class has two methods: one draws a rectangle on the screen, and the other calculates the area of the rectangle. Here, two applications use the Rectangle class.

item.title: Open-Closed Principle (OCP)
item.description:
The Open Closed Principle #

What Is the Open-Closed Principle (OCP)? #

The Open-Closed Principle (OCP) states that software entities (classes, modules, functions, etc.) should be open for extension but closed for modification.

With a “rigid” design, even a small change to a program affects every module that depends on the changed part. Applying the Open-Closed Principle lets you keep the impact of such modifications small.

item.title: Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)
item.description:
The Liskov Substitution Principle #

What Is the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)? #

The Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) states that subtypes must be substitutable for their base types. What happens if we do not follow this principle?

Suppose a function f takes as its argument a pointer or reference to some base class B. Now imagine there is a class D derived from B, and passing it to f in place of B causes f to misbehave. In that case, we say that class D violates the Liskov Substitution Principle.

item.title: Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)
item.description:
The Dependency Inversion Principle #

What Is the Dependency Inversion Principle? #

The Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) states that

  • High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on “abstractions”.
  • “Abstractions” should not depend on implementation details. Implementation details should depend on “abstractions”.

It is very common in traditional software development for high-level modules to depend on low-level modules. Take the common three-tier web architecture as an example: the Controller class depends on the Service class, and the Service class depends on the Repository class.

item.title: Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)
item.description:
The Interface Segregation Principle #

What Is the Interface Segregation Principle? #

The Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) states that clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use. This principle helps slim down “fat” interfaces. A class with a “fat” interface carries many interfaces, and those interfaces are only partially strongly related to each other. Looked at from another angle, this means that strongly related interfaces can be grouped together. Each group of member functions then serves a different client, because different clients need different member functions.
